message.content:
The total number of distinct positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated that the number of legal positions is on the order of

\[
10^{43}\text{–}10^{46}
\]

(roughly 10 to the 43rd to 46th power).  More recent computational estimates put the figure around \(10^{46}\) (about 1 × 10^46).  This is often called the “Shannon number” and represents the size of the search space that a chess engine would have to explore in the worst case.
